signals.excerpt:
# Introducing vLLM TorchTPU

October 20, 2026 6 min read

Table of Contents

Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU (`vllm-torchtpu`), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code.

This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to:

1. Make it easy to bring new models to TPU by reusing vLLM's existing model code.
2. Push TPU inference performance in open source, with Pallas kernels for attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and quantized matmul.
3. Keep the vLLM experience the same: the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler, and KV cache manager you use on other hardware.

...

### Models, Features, and What's Next

`vllm-torchtpu` can serve most models supported by vLLM, with TPU-specific kernel, quantization, and parallelism work for the Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS, and Gemma families. TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended hardware and is tested in CI on every pull request; v6e, v5e, and v5p are experimental.

The Supported Models & Features page has the full list of validated checkpoints and features, with how to enable each one. The nightly support matrices track TPU v7x correctness and benchmark results from CI.

signals.title: llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog

October 20, 2026

##### Mark Lohmeyer

Product Manager

##### Nov 4: Agentic Data Cloud Event

Today at the PyTorch Conference, we released llm-d 1.0, an open-source, Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Co-founded by Google with Red Hat, IBM and others, we worked with a community of more than 500 contributors over 25 organizations on this Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, bringing together two important communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production.

llm-d 1.0 arrives at a time when agents are changing the nature of inference. A year ago, most inference traffic was chat: one prompt in, one response out. Today, workloads are shifting to multi-step agents and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts that fan out across tools, share long prefixes, and arrive in bursts. Serving them on a single machine — or behind a generic round-robin load balancer — breaks down fast. Replicas recompute the same prompts, accelerator memory fills up with duplicate state, and one bursty agent loop can stall interactive users.

llm-d solves this for teams serving their own models by turning a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool. During the PyTorch Conference keynote, we showed this in action with 1,000 sandboxed agents on Agent Substrate on GKE hitting a single llm-d endpoint across vLLM, SGLang, and a mixed fleet of Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. As traffic scaled across the three stages below, cache-aware routing and tiered KV cache kept each agent's steps on the replicas holding its context, while flow control queued bursty agent loops so interactive requests stayed fast.

...

### What 1.0 provides

llm-d already delivered prefix- and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference across Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. These capabilities provide:

- Multi-tenant quality of service. Priority and fairness-aware routing via llm-d flow control, helping latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads share a fleet to meet SLOs without starving one another.
- A stable foundation. v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
- Safer upgrades. Router high availability and zero-downtime updates, alongside DisaggregatedSet, which orchestrates prefill/decode-aware rolling updates without dropping context or disrupting active sessions.
- Agent-aware serving. Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, and native Responses API state, helping agents reuse context across turns.
- Expanded TPU integration. Native PyTorch model serving with TorchTPU co-operative time-slicing to raise throughput and utilization across Google Cloud TPU fleets.

The components are designed so that you can compose them into your own bespoke production environment. Keep your engine, model and cluster, and adopt only the serving components and configurations you need.

...

One endpoint, many accelerators

An agent fleet is not one workload. Interactive turns need low latency, background loops and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts need high throughput, and demand swings by the minute. llm-d puts your accelerator pools behind a single endpoint, with one router, one KV cache index, and one flow-control policy in front of the whole fleet. Agents call a single API; the router picks the replica for each step and keeps a session's context on the replicas that already hold it. Adding capacity, mixing accelerator generations, or moving a model to a different pool becomes a platform change, not an agent rewrite. TorchTPU brings Google Cloud TPUs into that fleet, running PyTorch models natively inside upstream vLLM and SGLang without model rewrites. For more, see the llm-d on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) TPU guide.

...

Async inference that runs alongside real-time inference

For latency-tolerant traffic, llm-d 1.0 introduces llm-d-async-processor, which pulls requests from queues like Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis and routes them alongside real-time traffic. Using queue and pool-dispatch gates, the processor checks available capacity and enforces strict priority lanes and quotas so background jobs run in slack capacity without starving interactive users.

...

Teams serving their own models have been asking for an open stack they can take apart and adapt to their own infrastructure, with the cache-aware routing, traffic control, and upgrade controls required in production. llm-d 1.0 gives them that and a community to build with.

...

### Get started

1. Check out the full demo of llm-d with TPUs at the Google Cloud booth during the PyTorch Conference.
2. Deploy llm-d 1.0 on GKE with the verified Helm charts. See the llm-d on GKE documentation.
3. Start with prefix-aware routing in front of your existing vLLM deployment, then add flow control, KV cache offload (SGlang, vLLM) and disaggregation.
4. Compare results on Prism and contribute on GitHub.

signals.title: ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars
signals.excerpt:
# ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars

OpenViking from ByteDance's Volcengine treats agent memory, knowledge and skills as a virtual filesystem, crossing 40,000 GitHub stars.

 By Marcello Babbili · AI-assisted newsroom October 19, 2026 3 min read 

Image generated by OpenAI

ByteDance's Volcengine team published OpenViking, an open-source context database that treats everything an AI agent knows as files under a `viking://` filesystem, and the project crossed 40,000 stars on GitHub this week after gaining 105 stars in a single day on the platform's trending list S¹.

The approach challenges how most agent builders work today: stitching together separate systems for retrieval-augmented generation (the standard method for feeding documents into a model), conversation memory, and tool or skill management. OpenViking collapses all three into one virtual filesystem that an agent can browse and read on demand P² P⁴.

...

My read: This is the first agent-memory project I've seen that refuses to separate knowledge from memory from skills at the storage layer. Most teams I watch are still gluing a vector database to a chat-history buffer and calling it done. The filesystem metaphor is elegant, but the benchmark numbers are entirely self-reported and nobody outside the Volcengine team has verified them. I'd want to see independent tau2-bench results before believing the performance claims, and the 40,000-star count tells me about GitHub momentum, not production readiness.

...

### One filesystem, three context types

The Viking team, part of ByteDance's cloud infrastructure arm Volcengine, organises context into three types: resources for reference material, memories for information retained from interactions, and skills for task procedures P⁴. Each piece of context loads in three tiers: L0, a one-sentence abstract; L1, a core overview; and L2, the full original data S¹. An agent scans the L0 summaries to decide what it needs, then drills down to L2 only for relevant items, which keeps token consumption down.

When a conversation session ends, OpenViking commits and archives it as Markdown files that a developer can read and edit by hand S¹. Memories sit in readable text, not a binary store, which makes debugging and correction straightforward.

...

### The benchmarks nobody has checked

The project reports evaluation results on two benchmarks: LoCoMo, which tests long-conversation user memory, and tau2-bench, which tests multi-turn agent tasks S¹. Version 0.3.22 used Doubao 2.0 Pro, Volcengine's own vision-language model, for the memory evaluation S¹. These results are self-reported. The repository does not include peer-reviewed or third-party-audited benchmark data, and the README is the maintainers' description of their own work, not an independent review.

A developer who wants to try the system without committing to an install can use OpenViking Studio, a browser-based demo that requires no setup S¹.

The repository is written primarily in Python and carries the volcengine organisation label on GitHub, though the about page confirms the team sits inside ByteDance's Volcengine unit P².

Until an independent team reproduces the LoCoMo or tau2-bench results, the 40,000-star count measures interest, not proof.

# Meta Releases Muse Glimmer 30B: An Apache 2.0 Agentic Model That Runs on a Single Consumer GPU

Meta's Muse Glimmer is a 30B agentic model quantized to 4-bit for consumer GPUs, beating Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use and planning under Apache 2.0.

Automater Newsroom · October 19, 2026 at 6:44 PM ET

Muse Glimmer 30B: A 4-bit quantized 30B model that runs the full agentic loop — reasoning, tool use, and failure recovery — locally on a single consumer GPU, beating same-size competitors on agentic benchmarks.

Meta published the technical report for Muse Glimmer 30B on October 19, releasing the research page and paper under the Apache 2.0 license for an agentic model purpose-built to run autonomous tool-using agents on a single consumer GPU. The model integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use, and failure recovery into a single 30B-parameter package quantized to roughly 4-bit precision — small enough to fit on a GPU most developers already own. The model weights are not yet posted to Hugging Face at press time.

...

Meta's official Muse Glimmer 30B research page, published October 19, 2026. The abstract describes the model as an open-source Apache 2.0 agentic model with text and image inputs, 4-bit quantization for single-GPU inference, and state-of-the-art performance against Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B. Source: AI at Meta. · Original source

...

The primary source describes Muse Glimmer as a causal language model with a perception encoder that accepts both text and image inputs and produces text outputs. It was trained on data spanning over a hundred languages. The model is explicitly positioned for agentic workloads — multi-step planning, calling external tools, and recovering when those calls fail — rather than general chatbot or completion tasks.

The 4-bit quantization is the practical enabler. A 30B model at full precision would demand multiple high-end GPUs or cloud instances. At approximately 4-bit, Glimmer fits on a single consumer GPU, making local agentic inference viable without a data-center budget. For developers building always-on coding agents, research assistants, or automation workflows, that removes the per-token API meter entirely.

...

### What’s Not Yet Clear

The research page and its linked Arxiv paper provide the benchmark comparisons and architectural description, but Meta has not yet published the model weights on HuggingFace at the time of writing. The Meta Muse organization page on HuggingFace lists two image-text-to-text models at the 30B scale updated roughly 18 days ago, which may be earlier checkpoints or related releases. Developers should watch the organization page and Meta’s official channels for the weight drop.

signals.title: Crossing the threshold to dependable open source AI serving
signals.excerpt:
October 20, 2026 4-minute read AI inference, Artificial intelligence, Open source

 Brian Stevens SVP and CTO for AI 

When large open weight models first captured attention, the industry was faced with a challenge. Powerful open models were becoming available, but technologists lacked an open inference serving system that could run them efficiently. Having spent years building inference engines for CPUs, my team and I redirected all of our energy toward the vLLM project. Together with the community, vLLM capabilities expanded to become the de facto inference server. Today the vLLM project, now part of the PyTorch foundation, has a vibrant community of companies and developers actively adding support for new models, hardware, and research techniques.

As Red Hat continued this work, conversations with our enterprise users exposed a new reality. Getting a single server to perform efficiently was table stakes. The next challenge was orchestrating model serving at cluster scale. Last spring, we announced the llm-d project to address this, developing an open source, Kubernetes-native orchestration layer for distributed LLM serving across multi-tenant production clusters. Today, Red Hat and our community partners announced the release of llm-d 1.0. Reaching this milestone reflects a project hitting full maturity, shaped by hardened code, stability proven under real production load, and widespread adoption across an expanding contributor community. Open source AI serving has crossed from an experimental science project into dependable infrastructure you can build on.

...

Stability cannot be established on synthetic benchmarks alone. It has to survive real-world scale where agent contexts expand over hours of execution and accelerator memory faces unrelenting pressure. When multi-turn workloads repeatedly hit unmanaged clusters, naive load balancers scatter requests, wiping out cached prefix state and triggering massive recomputation costs.

llm-d delivers production-scale stability by making the orchestration layer aware of inference dynamics. It preserves context locality, disaggregates prefill from decode phases, and balances work across heterogeneous accelerator pools. In production, this operational stability creates dramatic efficiencies. At IBM Research, exploring quantum error correction hardware on llm-d generated multi-turn workloads with massive context reuse identical to agentic coding loops. That deployment yielded a 98% prefix-cache hit rate and reduced blended serving costs five to ten times compared to proprietary options.

In benchmark demonstrations, researchers used llm-d to deploy GLM-5.2, an approximately 753-billion-parameter open weight model on widely deployed NVIDIA GPUs, showcasing how enterprises can use existing GPU fleets to serve frontier-class AI at scale. On a workload with hundreds of agentic sessions running in parallel, llm-d delivered over 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak on agentic benchmarks. The cluster sustained up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents with zero preemptions, demonstrating that llm-d can efficiently serve large mixture-of-experts models for agentic workloads.

# Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog

Author: Qi Zhou, Chris Chan
Published: 2026-10-20T15:04:17Z
Source: developers.googleblog.com
Language: en

## Story

Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU - Google Developers Blog
# Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
OCT. 20, 2026
Qi Zhou Principal Software Engineer
Chris Chan Group Product Manager
As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).
## **Background**
For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.
So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.
Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.
## **The Inference Stack**
Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.
## **Engine Overview**
TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a `tpu` device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via `torch.compile` using XLA, and collectives go through `torch.distributed`.
Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager and API server etc, and add TPU implementations underneath.
Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in vLLM or SGLang, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace
### **Workload support**
Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.
Here’s the list of supported features:
* **Agentic & Multi-Turn:** Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
* **Interactive & Low Latency:** Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
* **High-throughput Batch:** Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
* **Long Context:** Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
* **Disaggregated Serving:** Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
* **Multimodal:** Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
* **Very Large Models:** Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints
Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.
### **Moving the KV Cache with TPU Sync**
Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.
Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.
## **Running today in production & public benchmarks**
Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.
Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall at 2.01 cents at high-concurrency configurations. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.
## **Building with the community**
We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:
**SGLang-TorchTPU was** **co-developed**** with RadixArk (founded by the creators of SGLang)**
This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.
*> "SGLang-TorchTPU is running in production at Meta today, and getting there was a close three-way collaboration between Meta, Google, and the SGLang team to make the stack production-ready. It gives us a remarkably mature, PyTorch-native serving stack that integrates effortlessly into our existing AI infrastructure, with the performance, reliability, and flexibility we need to run frontier workloads efficiently on TPUs. " said Zongwei Zhou, PyTorch-TPU lead at Meta.
*
*> "At RadixArk, TorchTPU has supercharged our development velocity as we roll out SGLang support across diverse silicon. It’s given us a painless path to native TPU acceleration, passing massive efficiency gains and flexible compute choices directly down to our customers," said Banghua Zhu, CTO and co-founder of RadixArk.
*
**vLLM-TorchTPU was** **co-developed**** with Inferact (founded by the creators of vLLM)**
Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.
*> "Our mission at Inferact has always been to make high-performance inference accessible, reliable, and cost-effective across the entire AI ecosystem. We are thrilled to partner on the launch of TorchTPU and bring first-class support for vLLM to TPUs. By bridging PyTorch’s optimized TPU capabilities directly into vLLM, developers can immediately run production workloads on TPUs with the high throughput, low latency, and memory efficiency they expect from our stack," said Simon Mo, CEO and co-founder of Inferact.
*
To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to both engines. Request here.
## **Roadmap**
As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!
Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma4 and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.
## **A note on our JAX runtimes**
vLLM-Jax, and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.
## **Getting started**
Get started today:
* vLLM-TorchTPU: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu
* SGLang-TorchTPU: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu
* TorchTPU: https://github.com/google-pytorch/torch\_tpu

# llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for day 2 production operations

The distributed inference framework makes serving large models on your own infrastructure reliable and affordable for the agentic era.

Today at the PyTorch Conference North America, llm-d project contributors are announcing llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for open-source AI infrastructure. A Kubernetes-native distributed inference serving network, llm-d makes it possible to deploy inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud.

The release signals that llm-d has moved beyond demonstrating individual performance techniques and is ready to support the realities of production: sustained efficiency under many workloads, all while balancing service priorities amid growing demand. And with inference costs increasing, llm-d is meant to help bring model deployment in-house and deliver returns on AI investment.

...

The result is a vendor-neutral alternative for organizations that want frontier-class inference performance without depending entirely on one proprietary model provider, cloud, or hardware platform.

...

## A full production stack

Since llm-d launched, the project has focused on five important approaches to improving AI inference: prefix-cache-aware routing, which directs a request to infrastructure that may already hold its shared context; KV-cache offloading, which expands the useful life of cached information by moving it across GPU, CPU, and storage resources; batch inference optimization, which groups work so infrastructure can process it more efficiently; prefill/decode disaggregation, which separates the work of reading a prompt from the work of generating a response; and wide expert parallelism, which distributes large mixture-of-experts models across many accelerators.

...

## One endpoint, different kinds of work

Expanding on the core technical innovations that have already made llm-d a powerful tool for distributed inference, llm-d 1.0 enhances support for multi-tenant quality of service, zero-downtime operations, and agent-aware serving, for sustained performance in common day 2 production operations. An enterprise AI service may receive requests from people and autonomous agents through the same endpoint, but those workloads behave differently. A person using a coding assistant expects a fast answer. An agent may send a large burst of requests, pause while using a tool, and then return for another round of model calls.

With flow control, llm-d 1.0 manages competing priorities whether workloads share the same hardware or span a mix of accelerators. Flow control, fairness, and prioritization help prevent bursty workloads from overwhelming latency-sensitive services. Under heavy demand, the system can make more deliberate decisions about which requests should receive resources first. Requests can also remain pinned to the appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns. That keeps their prefix caches warm, increasing the chance that previously processed context can be reused instead of calculated again.

This matters for conversational assistants, but it is especially valuable for agents. Agents frequently return to the same code, documents, instructions, and conversation history while carrying out a task. Prefix-cache-aware routing sends each turn toward a replica that already holds the relevant context, while KV-cache offloading helps preserve more of that reusable information when GPU memory becomes constrained. This is what production readiness looks like in practice: serving a model more effectively and more cost-effectively by understanding the work arriving at that model and managing infrastructure accordingly.

In a recent test of an agentic coding workload, llm-d’s prefix-aware router captured 97% of the available cache reuse. By avoiding repeated computation and making more efficient use of existing hardware, techniques like this can reduce the cost of serving AI at scale. signals.title: llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs
signals.excerpt:
llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs

Quantization Inference and serving· 17 Oct 2026

# llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs

Snapdragon devices get another notch of compression for on-device inference

## The facts

- Release b11716 of llama.cpp adds support for Q1_0 and Q2_0 quantisation formats on Qualcomm Hexagon NPUs (pull request #30122)
- Changes include enabling Q1_0 weights in the 2D HMX MUL_MAT path and adding Q2_0 support with cleanup of stale asserts and special cases
- Work includes fixes to the MUL_MAT_NX tiling assumption, since Q1/Q2 formats use non-square tiles rather than the square tiling assumed elsewhere
- Multiple commits optimise Q1_0 and Q2_0 vec_dots and layout to reduce unpack and vrmpy overhead
- Co-authored by Max Krasnyansky of Qualcomm; builds are available for Linux arm64 and Android arm64 targeting Snapdragon CPU, Adreno GPU and Hexagon NPU

The latest llama.cpp pre-release, tagged b11716, adds support for two low-bit quantisation formats on Qualcomm's Hexagon neural processing unit. Q1_0 and Q2_0 compress model weights to roughly one or two bits each. The change, merged via pull request #30122, lets the Hexagon backend run these compressed models through the existing 2D HMX matrix-multiply path used for tiled tensor formats.

Getting there required more than flipping a flag. Q1_0 and Q2_0 weights use non-square tiles, which broke an assumption baked into llama.cpp's MUL_MAT_NX routine: that tiling would always be square. The patch generalises that path instead of special-casing it. Several follow-up commits strip out stale asserts and special cases left over from earlier work. They also tighten the vec_dot routines and memory layout for both formats, cutting the overhead from unpacking and vector multiply-accumulate (vrmpy) operations.

The work was co-authored by Max Krasnyansky of Qualcomm. That underscores the chipmaker's continued hand in llama.cpp's Hexagon backend. Build artefacts for this release include a dedicated Linux arm64 target and an Android arm64 target. Both cover Snapdragon CPU, Adreno GPU and Hexagon NPU execution. The usual Linux, Windows, macOS and openEuler builds remain too, across CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, SYCL and OpenVINO backends.

...

## Why it matters

Sub-2-bit quantisation on Hexagon NPUs means developers can push larger models onto Snapdragon phones and laptops without falling back to the CPU or GPU path. Anyone targeting on-device inference on Snapdragon hardware should re-test memory and latency against this build before locking in a quant format.

# Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model

October 19, 2026

## Abstract

We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

signals.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands Beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Oct 19, 2026 2 min read 

by

- Sergio De Simone 

Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

> Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering.

Thanks to its multimodal capabilities, EmbeddingGemma 2 supports a wide range of retrieval tasks, including finding relevant documents, screenshots, and recordings in response to a query, searching source code using natural language, and retrieving video content based on textual descriptions.

EmbeddingGemma 2's key feature, Google says, is its ability to represent text, code, images, video, and audio in a unified 768-dimensional embedding space. This enables developers to build retrieval systems that search across different media types without maintaining separate, incompatible embedding spaces for different media types.

> Despite coming from different modalities, the embeddings generated by EmbeddingGemma 2 occupy the same dimensional space and can be compared on their semantic similarity.

The model allows developers to load only the encoders required for their applications, scaling from 270 million parameters for text and code to 740 million for full multimodal support. According to Google, the model "significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search".

...

EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), which allows embeddings to be truncated into shorter, unit-length vectors, reducing storage requirements. For example, storing a million 768-dimensional vectors at bfloat16 precision takes roughly 1.5 GB of memory, while truncating them to 128 dimensions requires just 250 MB, bringing a sixfold reduction. However, this implies a retrieval quality trade-off. Google therefore recommends using truncation only when storage or search speed require it. At 128 dimensions, the model retains approximately 90% of quality with text, but performance drops to around 75% for image, video, and speech retrieval.

...

EmbeddingGemma was introduced last year with a focus on "offline and privacy-sensitive scenarios, such as searching across personal files locally, running mobile RAG pipelines with Gemma 3n, or building domain-specific chatbots". EmbeddingGemma 2 is available on Hugging Face.

# 清华团队开源智能体操作系统PilotDeck 2.0，复杂任务成本降至约六分之一

清华大学THUNLP实验室联合面壁智能、OpenBMB等团队正式开源智能体操作系统PilotDeck 2.0。该系统以WorkSpace（工作舱）为基本单位，为不同任务提供独立的文件系统、记忆库和技能集，实现文件、记忆与任务的隔离，减少Agent执行任务时的上下文污染与记忆串台。

PilotDeck 2.0将记忆管理做成“白盒化”，用户可查看记忆生成、抽取、存储到调用的完整链路，并支持手动修改、删除或固定重要信息。系统内置Dream模式，在Agent空闲时自动对交互记忆进行归纳、提炼与去重，整理出错时可一键回滚。Always-on常驻执行模式允许Agent在用户关闭聊天窗口后继续后台推进长周期监控与执行任务，并生成进展报告。

该系统原生支持MCP（模型上下文协议），在Web界面、命令行CLI及企业微信、飞书等IM生态中保持后端逻辑一致，便于开发者扩展工具与技能。

在成本控制方面，PilotDeck通过Smart Routing智能路由进行任务难度识别与分层编排：复杂规划决策由强模型负责，底层执行、润色等交由轻量模型处理。在7个高难度复杂任务对比测试中，采用主模型Sonnet 4.6搭配子模型MiniMax-M2.7的“主强子弱”架构，综合得分高于单体顶配模型，成本约为后者的六分之一。在Workbuddy Bench评测中，PilotDeck使用Qwen3.6-35B-A3B得分79.1，优于Claude Code的77.3。

PilotDeck采用AGPL-3.0开源许可证，支持macOS、Linux和Windows，并提供Docker部署方式。

## What is in the release

DeepInfer bundles optimised code for DeepSeek’s models with ways to split the work across many chips. It also includes speculative decoding, a technique that drafts several tokens ahead and checks them in one pass. Other features keep outputs consistent from run to run and force answers into set formats, according to the GitHub page.

signals.title: Vercel Built a Durable Agent State Stack. The Reference App Is Open-Source and Running on AI Gateway.
signals.excerpt:
To address these constraints, Vercel is pivoting from ephemeral AI interactions toward a durable agent infrastructure stack. The objective is to standardize the lifecycle of agents that must operate over hours or days rather than seconds. By enforcing a clear separation of concerns—agent logic, execution environment, and persistence layer—the architecture moves developers away from stateless request-response patterns. Instead, it promotes stateful, event-driven systems capable of surviving the inherent instability of distributed computing.

...

At the center of this stack is fx0, an open-source, lightweight design agent released under the Apache-2.0 license that currently holds 228 stars. It serves as a reference implementation for the libfx library, which provides the core createFxAgent() and createFxEngine() APIs. The durability model is built on Vercel's World, a storage layer behind Vercel Workflow, where sessions are maintained. Every turn is backed by Vercel Queues, ensuring that a turn continues even if the underlying function dies. To manage resources, there is an 800-second maximum duration per invocation, with libfx programmed to stop 30 seconds before the limit to queue a continuation. Furthermore, a 64-step budget per turn is tracked in Redis to prevent subagents from inflating costs, and crash recovery is designed to take approximately 13 minutes.

...

The deeper issue is how these agents interact with data over time. Announced on October 15, 2026, at Vercel Ship 2026, Vercel Drives provides persistent file storage that survives sandbox shutdowns. Drives can be mounted by new sandboxes, forked for parallel exploration, or shared read-only across multiple agents. By integrating this with the AI Gateway, which handles model call billing through OAuth tokens or server trial keys, Vercel is creating a unified state management layer. This infrastructure complements other recent announcements, such as the eve framework for persistent memory, Vercel Connect, and the beta release of MCP Events.

...

For infrastructure builders and CTOs, this transition offers a path to reduce the complexity of multi-step agents. By offloading state persistence and recovery to the platform, developers can focus on agent logic rather than building custom backstops for function failures. However, this move also introduces new considerations. The reliance on a proprietary stack raises questions about vendor lock-in and the long-term interoperability of these agents with non-Vercel ecosystems. Additionally, as agent-triggered deployments continue to scale, the platform must prove it can maintain performance and reliability at significantly higher volumes than current levels.

signals.title: Arm Community
signals.excerpt:
October 19, 2026

# Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs

Learn how ExecuTorch brings PyTorch deployment to Arm Cortex-M CPUs with CMSIS-NN acceleration, low memory use, and support for embedded ML workflow today

...

ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server.

...

## The Cortex-M backend

Figure 1: ExecuTorch model compilation and deployment workflow for Arm Cortex-M CPUs.

The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm's CMSIS-NN library, an open-source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors.

Key properties:

- CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly.
- Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead.
- Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch's PT2E quantization framework.
- Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable.

...

Many Cortex-M MCUs pair the CPU with an Arm Ethos-U NPU such as the U55, U65, or U85. ExecuTorch's EthosUPartitioner delegates supported operations to the NPU via the Vela compiler, and operations left outside the partition run on the Cortex-M CPU within the same graph.

The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch's portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated.

...

In our measurements, ExecuTorch achieves 2.3% to 10.6% lower inference latency on three of the four models. Autoencoder latency is nearly identical, with ExecuTorch taking 0.27% longer. Memory is where the two frameworks diverge more sharply. The measured model/operator/core footprint is up to 21.1% less flash across all four models, and less RAM on three of the four, including 46.1% less on the Autoencoder. ResNet-8 is the exception, using 1.2% more RAM than TFLM.
